records.themeTitle: Natural powers depend on one hidden source
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok interprets the Sages’ language about harmful spiritual powers through their conviction that the Giver of nature governs nature itself. Particular effects have distinct hidden powers within the order of emanation, without becoming independent sources of life.
records.originHebrew: וּבְוַדַּאי הָיָה לָהֶם לְחַכְמֵיהֶם אָז לִדְבָרִים אֵלּוּ עִלּוֹת וּטְעָמִים יְדוּעִים עַל פִּי חָכְמַת הַטֶּבַע; אֲבָל רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה, שֶׁיָּדְעוּ שֶׁאֵין הַטֶּבַע הוּא הַמּוֹשֵׁל רַק נוֹתֵן הַטֶּבַע (וְעַיֵּן בִּתְשׁוּבַת חֲכַם צְבִי סִימָן י״ח), וּכְבָר נֶאֱמַר (אֵיכָה ג׳:ל״ח): "מִפִּי עֶלְיוֹן לֹא תֵצֵא הָרָעוֹת", רַק בְּהִשְׁתַּלְשְׁלוּת שׁוֹנוֹת כַּנּוֹדָע לְחַכְמֵי הָאֱמֶת, וְכֹחַ הַמַּזִּיק שֶׁבָּהֶם כְּפִי סֵדֶר הַהִשְׁתַּלְשְׁלוּת, יָדְעוּ שֶׁדְּבֵי פַרְחֵי הוּא "רוּחֵי", שֶׁהוּא מִצַּד הָרוּחַ לְבַד הַמַּזִּיק. וְכָךְ הָיָה יָדוּעַ גַּם לַטִּבְעִיִּים אָז, כִּי הָרוּחַ שֶׁבְּצִלּוֹ שֶׁל פַּרְחֵי מַזִּיק לָאָדָם. וּלְפִי שֶׁרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה יָדְעוּ שֶׁהַכֹּל בְּהִשְׁתַּלְשְׁלוּת מִלְּמַעְלָה וְיֵשׁ לוֹ כֹּחַ רוּחָנִי מַזִּיק, לָזֶה אָמְרוּ דְּשֵׁם הַמַּזִּיק "רוּחֵי",
records.originEnglish: The scholars of that time certainly had known causes and explanations for these things according to natural science. But our Sages, of blessed memory, knew that nature is not the ruler; the Giver of nature is (see the responsum of Chacham Tzvi, section 18). It has already been said, “From the mouth of the Most High, evils do not proceed” (Lamentations 3:38); rather, this occurs through different chains of emanation, as those versed in the true wisdom know. Knowing the harmful power within them according to the order of emanation, they knew that the power at the parcha tree was a ruach, a spirit, because the harm there came from the wind alone. The natural philosophers of that time likewise knew that the wind in the parcha tree’s shade was harmful to a person. Since our Sages knew that everything descends through an order of emanation from above and possesses a harmful spiritual power, they called that harmful power a ruach.
records.targetHebrew: וְאָמְנָם כֵּן, הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּעַצְמוֹ הוּא בֶּאֱמֶת הַמַּנְהִיג, כְּמוֹ שֶׁהַנֶּפֶשׁ אֶחָד כֵּן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אֶחָד, שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַיִּחוּד הָאֲמִתִּי הַיָּדוּעַ לַמַּאֲמִינִים. וְנִתְבָּאֵר אֶצְלֵנוּ בְּכַמָּה מְקוֹמוֹת בְּבֵאוּר אָרֹךְ עַל מַאֲמַר: "אַתָּה הוּא מִשֶּׁנִּבְרָא הָעוֹלָם, וְאַתָּה הוּא עַד שֶׁלֹּא נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם", שֶׁמַּמָּשׁ כְּמוֹ עַד שֶׁלֹּא נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם כֵּן הוּא מִשֶּׁנִּבְרָא, וְאֵין הַהֶבְדֵּל רַק לְמַרְאֵה עֵינֵי הַבְּרוּאִים הַמִּסְתַּכְּלִים בַּלְּבוּשׁ שֶׁהוּא הַבְּרִיאָה, שֶׁהוּא דֻּגְמַת לְבוּשׁ הַמַּעֲלֶה הַגּוּף, וּמַרְאֶה שֶׁיֵּשׁ שְׁנֵי דְבָרִים: בּוֹרֵא וְנִבְרָא, וְהַנִּבְרָא כְּאִלּוּ הוּא בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ וְנִבְדָּל מִן הַבּוֹרֵא. וּמִצַּד הַהֶעְלֵם יֵשׁ גַּם כֵּן אֶל הַנֶּפֶשׁ, שֶׁעִם הֱיוֹת בִּהְיוֹתָהּ חוּץ לַגּוּף הִיא אַחַת לְבַד, כַּאֲשֶׁר בָּאָה תּוֹךְ הַגּוּף שֶׁהוּא הַלְּבוּשׁ הִיא מִתְחַלֶּקֶת בְּתוֹךְ הַלְּבוּשׁ לִשְׁלֹשָׁה, שֶׁכָּל אַחַת כּוֹלֵל כָּל כֹּחוֹתֶיהָ, וְכָל אַחַת בְּגִלּוּי יוֹתֵר; וְהַכֹּל מִצַּד הַלְּבוּשׁ הַנִּרְאֶה כְּדָבָר מְחֻלָּק מִן הָעֶצֶם, שֶׁזֶּהוּ תַּכְלִית עִנְיַן מַהוּת הַבְּרִיאָה שֶׁהוּא נְתִינַת מָקוֹם לְהַרְאוֹת שֶׁיֵּשׁ דָּבָר מֻבְדָּל מִן הָעֶצֶם. וְאִם כֵּן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁבַּנֶּפֶשׁ כְּשֶׁהִיא מְלֻבֶּשֶׁת בַּגּוּף, שֶׁהוּא הַנֶּפֶשׁ מִצַּד שֶׁהִיא בַּבְּרִיאָה שֶׁהַגּוּף עַכְשָׁו נִבְרָא בְּעֵת הַהוֹלָדָה, הִיא שְׁלֹשָׁה כֹחוֹת, וְנִמְצָא אֵלּוּ הַשְּׁלֹשָׁה כֹחוֹת שֶׁל מַחֲשָׁבָה, דִּבּוּר וּמַעֲשֶׂה הֵם בֶּאֱמֶת כְּמוֹ לְבוּשִׁים לְעֶצֶם הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַיְּחִידָה וְכוֹלֶלֶת כֻּלָּם; כֵּן כִּבְיָכוֹל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בַּבְּרִיאָה שֶׁרָצָה וְחָשַׁב לַעֲשׂוֹת, שֶׁהוּא כְּמוֹ הוֹלָדָה שֶׁנּוֹלַד גּוּף שָׁלֵם מְחֻלָּק לְג׳ כֹּחוֹת, כָּל אַחַת מְגַלָּה יוֹתֵר הַכֹּחוֹת שֶׁבּוֹ. וְעַצְמוּת כֹּחַ הַכֹּחוֹת הָהֵם הוּא מִן הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַיְּחִידָה; אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם הַכֹּחוֹת בְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הֵם מְחֻלָּקִים לִשְׁלֹשָׁה חֲלָקִים שׁוֹנִים, שֶׁהֵם: הָאֶחָד בְּהֶעְלֵם, וְהַשֵּׁנִי גַּם כֵּן בְּהֶעְלֵם אֲבָל בְּגִלּוּי קְצָת יוֹתֵר לְכֹחוֹת הָאֵבָרִים עַל כָּל פָּנִים, וְהַשְּׁלִישִׁי בְּגִלּוּי יוֹתֵר גָּמוּר. וְאָנָה מָצָאנוּ גַּם כֵּן בִּבְרִיאַת הָעוֹלָם כֵּן? שֶׁאֲנַחְנוּ רוֹאִים רַק הַגָּלוּי, וְעַל כָּרְחָךְ שֶׁיֵּשׁ עוֹד נֶעְלָם, וְנֶעְלָם לַנֶּעְלָם.
records.targetEnglish: Indeed, Hashem Himself is truly the one who governs. Just as the soul is one, so Hashem is one: this is the true unity known to believers. We have explained at length in several places the statement, “You are He since the world was created, and You are He before the world was created”: it is precisely the same since creation as before creation. The difference exists only to the eyes of created beings, who look at the garment that is creation. It resembles a garment covering the body and makes it appear that there are two things, Creator and creature, with the creature seemingly existing in its own right, apart from its Creator. Concealment also applies to the soul. Although outside the body it is one alone, when it enters the body, which is its garment, it is divided within that garment into three powers; each contains all its powers, and each reveals them more openly. All this comes from the garment, which appears separate from the essence. This is the purpose of the very nature of creation: to allow something to appear distinct from the essence. Thus, when the soul is clothed in the body—that is, when it is within creation, the body now being created at birth—it has three powers. These three powers of thought, speech, and action are therefore truly like garments for the single soul that includes them all. So too, as it were, with Hashem in the creation He willed and conceived to make: it is like a birth in which a complete body is born, divided into three powers, each revealing its powers more openly. The essential power of these powers comes from the single soul. Nevertheless, in their extension the powers are divided into three different parts: one concealed, a second also concealed but somewhat more revealed to the powers of the organs, and a third more fully revealed. Where do we find this also in the creation of the world? We see only the revealed; necessarily there is also what is concealed, and what is concealed from the concealed.
records.explanation: Sichat Malakhei HaSharet explains how distinct hidden powers can operate while their source remains one. The soul’s thought, speech, and action provide the analogy: different degrees of manifestation do not create several independent souls. This supplies the conceptual structure behind Sichat Shedim’s insistence that the Sages could describe a particular spiritual power while attributing the governance of nature to its Giver.
records.translationProvenance: New English translations prepared for this conceptual connection, checked phrase by phrase against the quoted canonical Hebrew. Both complete sections of Sichat Shedim and each complete target paragraph were read; relevance, context, and quotation boundaries were reviewed separately from integrity tests.

records.themeTitle: Human action carries the life of creation
records.themeSummary: In explaining why human conduct affects forces beyond the person, Rav Tzadok presents Adam as a unifying source of life for the lower creation. Adam’s ability to name the creatures expresses a knowledge of their life through his own.
records.originHebrew: וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר, כִּי כָל מַה שֶּׁבָּעוֹלָם הוּא מִצַּד מַעֲשֵׂה בְנֵי אָדָם עַל יְדֵי פְּעֻלּוֹתָיו שֶׁהֵם נִמְשָׁכִים מֵחִיּוּתוֹ, עַל יְדֵי זֶה הוּא חִיּוּת כָּל הַנִּבְרָאִים שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עַל פָּסוּק: "הֵן הָאָדָם הָיָה כְּאַחַד מִמֶּנּוּ" [בְּרֵאשִׁית ג׳:כ״ב] — מַה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא יָחִיד בָּעֶלְיוֹנִים, אַף אָדָם בַּתַּחְתּוֹנִים; מַשְׁמָע מַמָּשׁ דֻּגְמָתוֹ, כְּמוֹ כִּבְיָכוֹל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא חִיּוּת כָּל הָעֶלְיוֹנִים, אַף הוּא כָךְ חִיּוּת כָּל הַתַּחְתּוֹנִים. וּלְכָךְ הוּא יָחִיד בָּהֶם, הַיְינוּ יָחִיד וּמְיֻחָד שֶׁחִיּוּתוֹ וְחִיּוּתָם אֶחָד. וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עַל פָּסוּק: "וַיִּקְרָא לָהֶם שֵׁמוֹת" [בְּרֵאשִׁית ב׳:כ׳], דְּמַלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת לֹא יָדְעוּ זֶה; וְהַיְינוּ דִּשְׁמוֹ הוּא חִיּוּתוֹ, וְחִיּוּת כֻּלָּם נִמְשָׁךְ מִמֶּנּוּ, לְכָךְ הוּא יָדַע מִפְּנֵי שֶׁיָּדַע אֶת עַצְמוֹ.
records.originEnglish: As I have written elsewhere, everything in the world comes about through human deeds: through a person’s actions, which proceed from his life, he is the life of all the creatures in the world. As our Sages said about the verse, “Behold, the human has become like one of us” (Genesis 3:22): just as the Holy One, blessed be He, is unique among the higher beings, so the human is among the lower beings. This implies an actual likeness: just as the Holy One, blessed be He, is, as it were, the life of all the higher beings, so the human is the life of all the lower beings. Therefore he is unique among them—unique and unifying, because his life and their life are one. As our Sages said about “He gave them names” (Genesis 2:20), the ministering angels did not know this. A creature’s name is its life; the life of them all flows from him, and therefore he knew it because he knew himself.

records.targetEnglish: “God said: Let us make a human.” At first Hashem, blessed be He, created all the creatures. Afterward, the creatures understood and recognized their lack: they had no one to connect their life to Hashem, blessed be He. Through the human, all the things of this world are connected to Hashem, for he raises everything, as is known. The mineral gives its power to the plant, the plant to the animal, and the animal to the speaking human. When the human serves Hashem with his strength, he raises all the powers he has received from this world, including the power of the mineral. When the creatures saw what they lacked, they brought about, through their power, an awakening above for the creation of the human. “God said: Let us make a human” means that Hashem told all the creatures to contribute from their power and join in creating the human, so that he would have a share in them all. Then, if the human needed something, they would all stand ready to help him, because harm to him would harm them too, as in the generation of the Flood, and his good would be their good too.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach describes the chain by which the powers of the lower creation enter human life and are raised when a person uses them in divine service. This makes the claim that human action affects all creatures more concrete: human life contains their powers, and its use determines what happens to those powers. The connection also preserves the ultimate direction of that unification—toward Hashem—rather than treating the human as an independent creator.

records.themeTitle: Final repair transforms the root of evil
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok argues that evil cannot achieve an independent, wholly evil completion. Shabbat and Adam’s repentance anticipate the final return to the source, when the creatures remain but their impurity is removed.
records.originHebrew: וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁבִּגְמַר מַעֲשֶׂה אֵין כָּאן רַע בֶּאֱמֶת, כִּי סוֹף הַכֹּל לְטוֹבָה, וְ"חָשַׁב מַחֲשָׁבוֹת לְבִלְתִּי יִדַּח [מִמֶּנּוּ נִדָּח]" [שְׁמוּאֵל ב י״ד:י״ד], וְאֵין כָּאן גּוּף רַע בֶּאֱמֶת כְּלָל. וְזֶה סוֹד מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ: "שֶׁקֶר אֵין לוֹ רַגְלַיִם" בְּשַׁבָּת (ק״ד עַמּוּד א׳), וּמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (ו׳ עַמּוּד א׳) וְהַנִּיזָּקִין [גִּטִּין ס״ח עַמּוּד ב׳] שֶׁרַגְלֵי הַשֵּׁדִים כְּתַרְנְגוֹלִים, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ לְהַאֲרִיךְ. וְהָיָה זֶה עַל יְדֵי יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת שֶׁהוּא תִּקּוּן אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה שֶׁאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן אָמַר מִזְמוֹר שֶׁל יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת, שֶׁאָז נִתְקַבְּלָה תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ, וְכֵן יִהְיֶה בְּסוֹף הַכֹּל הַתִּקּוּן שֶׁחוֹזֵר לִמְקוֹרוֹ, וְאֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מַנִּיחַ שֶׁיִּשְׁתַּלֵּם הָרָע, וּלְכָךְ אֵין שׁוּם בְּרִיָּה שֶׁיְּהֵא רַע גָּמוּר, רַק הַכֹּל מְעֹרָב טוֹב וָרָע. וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא בְּשַׁבָּת (ע״ז עַמּוּד ב׳) שֶׁהַכֹּל יֵשׁ בּוֹ תּוֹעֶלֶת; וְכֵן לֶעָתִיד יְתֻקַּן הַכֹּל וְלֹא יֶחְסַר שׁוּם בְּרִיָּה מִן הָעוֹלָם: "וְגָר זְאֵב [עִם כֶּבֶשׂ]" [יְשַׁעְיָהוּ י״א:ו׳], "וְנָחָשׁ [עָפָר לַחְמוֹ]" [שָׁם ס״ה:כ״ה];
records.originEnglish: At the completion of action, there is in truth no evil here, for the end of everything is for good, and He “devises means so that no banished one is banished from Him” (II Samuel 14:14). There is therefore no truly evil body at all. This is the secret of the saying, “Falsehood has no legs” (Shabbat 104a), and of the statements in Berakhot 6a and in HaNizakin (Gittin 68b) that the feet of demons are like those of roosters; this is not the place to elaborate. This came about through Shabbat, which is the repair of Adam. As our Sages said, Adam recited the psalm for Shabbat, when his repentance was accepted. So too, at the end of everything, repair will return to its source. The Holy One, blessed be He, does not allow evil to reach completion; therefore no creature is wholly evil, but everything is a mixture of good and evil. As stated in Shabbat 77b, everything has some benefit. Likewise, in the future everything will be repaired, and no creature will be missing from the world: “The wolf will dwell with the lamb” (Isaiah 11:6), and “The serpent—dust shall be its food” (Isaiah 65:25).
records.targetHebrew: בְּעִקְּבָתָא דִּמְשִׁיחָא הָעִיקָּר הוּא רַק לְהוֹצִיא יָקָר מִזּוֹלֵל, וְרַק בִּמְקוֹם יֵצֶר הָרָע וְתִגְבֹּורֶת עֲווֹנוֹת מִשָּׁם יִקָּחֲךָ דַּיְיקָא עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (צח.): בֶּן דָּוִד בָּא בְּדוֹר שֶׁכֻּלּוֹ חַיָּיב. וְנֶפֶשׁ כָּזֶה הוּא מֵחֶלְקוֹ שֶׁל מָשִׁיחַ, וְכֵן דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נִקְרָא שֶׁהֵקִים עוֹלָהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה. כִּידוּעַ דִּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל "רַגְלֶיהָ יֹרְדוֹת וְכוּלֵי" רַחֲמָנָא לִצְלַן; וּבְעִקְבֵי מָשִׁיחַ הַנְּפָשׁוֹת מִן הָרַגְלִין, וְשָׁם תִּגְבֹּורֶת הָרָע וְהַיֵּצֶר. וּלְכָךְ דּוֹר שֶׁל נְפָשׁוֹת כָּאֵלּוּ דַּיְיקָא יִזְכּוּ לְמָשִׁיחַ, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ט): "טוֹב מְאֹד" – זֶה יֵצֶר הָרָע. וְכֵן מָשִׁיחַ עַצְמוֹ נוֹלַד מִמָּקוֹם כָּזֶה, כִּידוּעַ מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בְּמִדְרַשׁ הַנֶּעֱלָם וַיֵּרָא עַל בְּנוֹת לוֹט וְלוֹט, שֶׁהֵם שׁוֹרֶשׁ כֹּחַ הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע, וּמִשָּׁם נִצְמַח שׁוֹרֶשׁ בֶּן דָּוִד. וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁזֶּהוּ תַּכְלִית הַשְּׁלֵימוּת שֶׁיִּהְיֶה אָז: שֶׁיִּתְהַפֵּךְ שׁוֹרֶשׁ הָרַע לְטוֹב, שֶׁזֶּה שְׁחִיטַת הַיֵּצֶר שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֻכָּה (נב.). וְהוּא הַנֶּפֶשׁ הָאַחֲרוֹן שֶׁבַּגּוּף, וְהַיּוֹתֵר סָמוּךְ לָרַע בְּכָל מִינֵי תֹּקֶף. וּבָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַדּוֹרוֹת הוֹלְכִים וּמִתְקַטְּנִים, אֲבָל אָז כְּשֶׁיְּתוּקַּן, יִהְיֶה בְּטוֹב "סוֹף מַעֲשֶׂה בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה תְּחִלָּה", בְּסוֹד הַחַיּוֹת: "רָצוֹא וָשׁוֹב כְּמַרְאֵה הַבָּזָק", שֶׁמִּמָּקוֹם שֶׁפּוֹסֵק, מִשָּׁם חוֹזֵר וּמַתְחִיל לְהָאִיר, וְנַעֲשָׂה זֶה רֹאשׁ, וְנִתְהַפְּכוּ תַּחְתּוֹנִים לְמַעְלָה, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (פְּסָחִים נ.): "עוֹלָם הָפוּךְ רָאִיתִי":
records.targetEnglish: In the footsteps of the Messiah, the essential task is only to bring forth the precious from the worthless. Precisely from the place of the evil inclination and the intensification of sins, He will take you through repentance, as stated in Chelek (Sanhedrin 98a): the son of David comes in a generation that is entirely guilty. Such a soul belongs to the portion of the Messiah. David, peace be upon him, is likewise called the one who established the yoke of repentance. As is known, concerning the Congregation of Israel, “her feet descend,” and so forth—may the Merciful One protect us. In the footsteps of the Messiah, the souls come from the feet, where evil and the inclination are strongest. Therefore precisely a generation of such souls will merit the Messiah, as our Sages said (Bereishit Rabbah, chapter 9): “Very good”—this is the evil inclination. The Messiah himself likewise comes from such a place: as is known from the Midrash HaNeelam, Vayera, concerning Lot and his daughters, who are the root of the power of the evil inclination; from there grew the root of the son of David. This is the ultimate perfection that will then come about: the root of evil will be transformed into good. This is the slaughter of the inclination spoken of in Sukkah 52a. It is the last soul in the body, the closest to evil in every kind of intensity. In this world the generations grow progressively smaller. But then, when repair takes place, “the end of action is first in thought” will be fulfilled for good, in the mystery of the living creatures’ “running and returning, like the appearance of lightning.” Where it ceases, from there it returns and begins to shine; this becomes the head, and those below are turned upward, as our Sages said (Pesachim 50a), “I saw an inverted world.”
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik describes the final return in the language of souls and repentance. What is nearest to evil becomes the starting point of renewed illumination when its root is transformed into good. This explains why Sichat Shedim can speak of repair without the disappearance of creatures: the change concerns the direction and quality of their life. Repentance remains explicit in both passages; the promised repair is not an approval of wrongdoing.

records.themeTitle: Different corrupt powers require different remedies
records.themeSummary: Sichat Shedim arranges the three severe transgressions along the right, left, and central lines. Desire and violent anger are branches that can lead to the corruption of the central body; their different positions matter for how they are repaired.
records.originHebrew: אֲבָל דַּע, כִּי כָל דָּבָר מִתְחַלֵּק לִג׳ קַוִּין: שְׁנֵי קְצוֹת וְאֶמְצָעִי כַּנּוֹדָע, וְהֵם בַּסְּפִירוֹת: חֶסֶד, גְּבוּרָה, תִּפְאֶרֶת; וְנֶגְדָּם בַּקְּלִפָּה: עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, גִּלּוּי עֲרָיוֹת, שְׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים. עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה הוּא קַו אֶמְצָעִי, וְהוּא תִּפְאֶרֶת דִּקְלִפָּה הַנִּמְשָׁךְ מִן הַכֶּתֶר, שֶׁהוּא הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ שֶׁרָצָה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נִמְצָא שֶׁיִּרְצֶה לְהִתְדַּמּוֹת לוֹ, וְזֶהוּ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה. וְקָצֶה הַיְמָנִי — גִּלּוּי עֲרָיוֹת, שֶׁהוּא תַּאֲוָה וְאַהֲבָה רָעָה, וְכַנּוֹדָע מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר בַּאֲחוֹתוֹ: "חֶסֶד הוּא" [וַיִּקְרָא כ׳:י״ז]; וּגְבוּרָה רָעָה הוּא לִשְׁפֹּךְ דָּם נָקִי בִּגְבוּרָתוֹ. וּמָצִינוּ שְׁתֵּי פְעָמִים בְּדִבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: כָּךְ דַּרְכּוֹ שֶׁל יֵצֶר הָרָע: הַיּוֹם אוֹמֵר לוֹ כָּךְ עַד שֶׁאוֹמֵר לוֹ עֲבֹד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה: הָאֶחָד בְּשַׁבָּת (ק״ה עַמּוּד ב׳) גַּבֵּי מְשַׁבֵּר כֵּלָיו בַּחֲמָתוֹ, דְּהַיְינוּ אֲבִיזְרַיְיהוּ דִּשְׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים; וְהַשֵּׁנִי בְּנִדָּה (י״ג עַמּוּד ב׳) גַּבֵּי מֵבִיא עַצְמוֹ לִידֵי הִרְהוּר, שֶׁהוּא אֲבִיזְרַיְיהוּ דְּגִלּוּי עֲרָיוֹת. וְהֵם קְצֵה הַיָּדוֹת, וְהַיָּדוֹת הֵם עֲנָפִים מֵהַגּוּף, וְעַל יָדוֹ יָבוֹא לְמַעְלָה עַד הַגּוּף שֶׁהוּא עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה.
records.originEnglish: Know that everything divides into three lines: two extremes and a middle, as is known. In the sefirot these are Chesed, Gevurah, and Tiferet, and opposite them in the husk are idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, and bloodshed. Idolatry is the middle line, the Tiferet of the husk that proceeds from Keter—the root that Hashem willed to exist, that would wish to resemble Him; this is idolatry. The right extreme is forbidden sexual relations, which is desire and corrupt love, as is known from what is said concerning one’s sister: “It is chesed” (Leviticus 20:17). Corrupt Gevurah is shedding innocent blood through one’s might. Twice in our Sages’ words we find: such is the way of the evil inclination—today it tells him one thing, until it tells him to worship idols. One is in Shabbat 105b, concerning someone who breaks his vessels in anger, an associated form of bloodshed. The other is in Niddah 13b, concerning someone who brings himself to sexual thoughts, an associated form of forbidden sexual relations. These are the extremities of the arms; the arms are branches of the body, and through them one rises toward the body, which is idolatry.
records.targetHebrew: כִּי זֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה עָשָׂה אֱלֹהִים, שְׁלֹשָׁה כֹּחוֹת הָרַע הֵם עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, גִּילּוּי עֲרָיוֹת, וּשְׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים. וְיָדוּעַ: הָעוֹמֵד לְעוּמַּת חֲבֵירוֹ יָמִין זֶה נֶגֶד שְׂמֹאל זֶה וְכוּלֵי (עַיֵּין רַעְיָא מְהֵימְנָא זוֹהַר חֵלֶק ג, רמו עַמּוּד ב). וְזֶהוּ "יִפֹּל וְגוֹמֵר", דְּהַשְּׂמֹאל דְּהַיְינוּ יִרְאַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הִיא מַפֶּלֶת תַּאֲווֹת רָעוֹת. וּכְמְפוֹרָשׁ בַּכָּתוּב: "כִּי אָמַרְתִּי רַק אֵין יִרְאַת וְגוֹמֵר", כִּי הַשְּׁקוּעִים בְּתַאֲוָה אֵין יִרְאָה נֶגֶד פְּנֵיהֶם. וּלְכָךְ הַיִּרְאָה הִיא תַּרְעָא לְאָעָלָא וְכוּלֵי (זוֹהַר חֵלֶק א, יא עַמּוּד ב), הַיְינוּ הַהַתְחָלָה בְּיַלְדוּת דְּאָז יֵצֶר הַתַּאֲווֹת בּוֹעֵר. "וְיִפֹּל" – רַק אֶלֶף, כִּי אָמְרוּ (סוֹטָה מז.): "יֵצֶר וְכוּלֵי וְיָמִין מְקָרֶבֶת". אֲבָל "רְבָבָה מִימִינֶךָ" עַל יְדֵי אַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הַגּוֹרֶמֶת אַהֲבַת יִשְׂרָאֵל וְדוֹחָה רְצִיחָה וָכַעַס וְקִנְאָה וַאֲבִיזְרַיְיהוּ, וּלְאֵלּוּ הִיא דּוֹחָה לְגַמְרֵי דְּאֵין בָּזֶה קֵירוּב כְּלָל. records.targetEnglish: For God has made one opposite the other. The three powers of evil are idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, and bloodshed. As is known, when one person stands facing another, the right of one faces the left of the other, and so forth (see Raaya Mehemna, Zohar III, 246b). This is the meaning of “A thousand shall fall,” and so forth: the left, which is fear of Hashem, casts down corrupt desires. As Scripture states explicitly, “For I said: there is no fear of God,” and so forth, because those immersed in desire have no fear before their eyes. Therefore fear is the gateway through which one enters, and so forth (Zohar I, 11b): it is the beginning in youth, when the inclination toward desires burns. But “shall fall” is only a thousand, for they said (Sotah 47a), concerning the inclination and so forth, “the right hand draws near.” By contrast, “ten thousand at your right”: love of Hashem causes love of Israel and repels murder, anger, jealousy, and their associated forms. It rejects these entirely; there is no drawing near for them. “Ten thousand shall fall” is an expression of exceedingly great abundance. A thousand, although also a large number used hyperbolically in several places, still belongs to the category of number, for a thousand is the largest concluding number in biblical language. But revavah, “ten thousand,” expresses abundance beyond the category of number—that is, without limit. There, however, the casting down is limited: when it reaches boundless abundance, which is the level of the right, it draws near. This is the meaning of “If [this vile one] encounters you, draw him into the house of study” (Sukkah 52b): not cast him away, but draw him there. For Torah is a seasoning, like something that seasons what is foul, making it good and giving it a praiseworthy taste.
records.explanation: Resisei Layla uses the same three-line structure to explain the work of repair. Fear restrains corrupt desire, while love of Hashem and Israel rejects anger and violence; desire also has a dimension that Torah can draw near and transform. This shows why the distinction between the two arms in Sichat Shedim is consequential: the branches do not receive one identical treatment, even though both can lead toward the corrupted center.

records.themeTitle: Torah reaches the force within desire
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok distinguishes desire, which has a necessary role in the continuation of life, from anger considered in itself. He locates the repair of a defect in the power of desire in Torah’s wisdom, rather than describing the force itself as something simply to erase.

records.originEnglish: At his right is the wise heart, for Chesed proceeds from Chokhmah in a straight line, as is known; likewise, the drops of seed come from the brain. Therefore the holy Zohar says that repentance does not avail for wasting seed: repentance is in Binah, as is known, as it is said, “His heart will understand, and he will return” (Isaiah 6:10). Its essence is the heart’s devotion, while the defect is in Chokhmah, which is above Binah. Therefore its repair is only through Torah, which also comes from Chokhmah, as I have written elsewhere. Gevurah comes from Binah, as it is said, “Anger from your heart.” Gevurah is good only in the Torah scholar, as stated above—that is, when it proceeds from Chokhmah, from the right chamber of the heart; at the left it is always the heart of a fool. At the right is the wise heart proceeding from Chokhmah. Therefore desire is situated in the heart of the living being, and it contains good: the continuation of the species and the birth of souls essentially depend on it. Concerning this they said (Bereishit Rabbah 9:7), “Very good”—this is the evil inclination. Therefore they said in Yoma 69b that they could not abolish it, for this reason.

records.targetEnglish: If he defeats it, good; if not, let him engage in Torah. When he has considered that this desire will not be his forever, yet still longs for it, it appears to some degree to be an enduring desire. But he must still perform the second discernment: to engage in Torah. Words of Torah are counsel for a person to be saved from desire, even at the time of the evil inclination, when no one remembers the good inclination (Nedarim 32b). For this the Holy One, blessed be He, created Torah as a seasoning. In truth, when a person is immersed in desire and cannot escape it, remembering that the thing is forbidden is no remedy, because at the time of the evil inclination the prohibition does not have sufficient power to separate him from evil. The counsel then is to remember that he can find this very good in words of Torah, in holiness. As explained concerning “The sea saw and fled”: it saw that Hashem can turn rock into a pool of water and flint into a spring of water. It would seem that the opposite should have been written—that it saw Hashem’s might to destroy and dry up the sea. But the sea alludes to desire. When desire intensifies, the only counsel against it is to show that the same thing exists in holiness; then it ceases.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach supplies a practical account of Torah’s action upon desire: it discloses the sought good in holiness, where a reminder of prohibition alone may fail to move the person. This illuminates Sichat Shedim’s account of a repair reaching the wisdom from which desire proceeds. The target’s full paragraph continues with further tests through the Shema and remembrance of death; its recognition of desire’s possible holy content does not by itself authorize acting upon it.

records.themeTitle: Revealed rule remains one with its hidden source
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok distinguishes two theological errors: removing divine governance from the higher source, and treating governance in this world as a separate power. Anokhi and Lo Yihye address these two separations.
records.originHebrew: וְהֵם לְשָׁרֵשׁ שְׁנֵי מִינֵי טָעוּיוֹת הַנִּזְכָּרִים לְעֵיל: "אָנֹכִי" — נֶגֶד כּוֹפֵר בָּעִקָּר, דְּפֵרְשׁוּ בַּתִּקּוּנִים שָׁם: מַאן דְּנָטֵיל תְּשַׁע סְפִירוֹת בְּלֹא מַלְכוּת; רָצָה לוֹמַר, שֶׁאוֹמֵר: לֵית דִּין וְלֵית דַּיָּן, זֶהוּ מַכְחִישׁ בְּמִדַּת מַלְכוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁבַּכֹּל מָשָׁלָה וְשַׁלִּיט בְּעוֹלָמוֹ, וְ"אָנֹכִי אֱלֹהֶיךָ" — מַנְהִיגְךָ וּמַשְׁגִּיחַ וְעוֹשֶׂה כִּרְצוֹנוֹ. וּ"מְקַצֵּץ בִּנְטִיעוֹת" — הַיְינוּ מַלְכוּת בְּלֹא תְּשַׁע סְפִירוֹת, הַיְינוּ אֱמוּנַת אֵל אַחֵר הַנְהָגָה וּמֶמְשָׁלָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁאֵינָהּ נִמְשֶׁכֶת מִמְּקוֹר חִיּוּת הָעֶלְיוֹן יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁזֶּהוּ תְּשַׁע סְפִירוֹת, הַמְשָׁכַת הֲוָיָ״ה כֻּלָּהּ וְסֵדֶר הַהִשְׁתַּלְשְׁלוּת מִן הָאֵין סוֹף. וְכֵן אָמְרוּ בַּחֲגִיגָה (ט״ו עַמּוּד ב׳): אַחֵר קִצֵּץ בִּנְטִיעוֹת, שֶׁאָמַר: שְׁתֵּי רְשֻׁיּוֹת הֵן.
records.originEnglish: They uproot the two kinds of error mentioned above. “I am” opposes denying the root, which the Tikkunim there explains as taking nine sefirot without Malkhut. This means saying that there is no judgment and no judge: it denies His attribute of kingship, which rules over everything and governs His world. “I am your God” means: your guide, who watches over you and acts according to His will. “Cutting the plantings” means Malkhut without the nine sefirot: belief in another god, a governance and dominion in this world that does not proceed from the source of supernal life, blessed be He. The nine sefirot are the entire extension of the divine name and the order of emanation from the Infinite. Thus they said in Chagigah 15b that Acher cut the plantings, saying that there were two authorities.
records.targetHebrew: פַּעַם אַחַת בְּיוֹם טוֹב רִאשׁוֹן שֶׁל פֶּסַח חָלַם לִי פֵּרוּשׁ לְשׁוֹן הַהַגָּדָה: "אֲנִי הוּא וְלֹא אַחֵר": רָצָה לוֹמַר דַּרְגָּא דַּ"אֲנִי", שֶׁהוּא מַדְרֵגָה הַיּוֹתֵר תַּחְתּוֹנָה, סוֹד הַשְּׁכִינָה [הַשּׁוֹכֵן בְּתוֹךְ הַלְּבָבוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל עַד שֶׁיָּכוֹל לוֹמַר בְּשֵׁם ה' לְשׁוֹן "אֲנִי"] כַּנּוֹדָע, הוּא עַצְמוֹ דַּרְגָּא דְּ"הוּא", שֶׁהוּא מַדְרֵגָה הַיּוֹתֵר עֶלְיוֹנָה הַנֶּעְלֶמֶת, סוֹד כֶּתֶר עֶלְיוֹן [וּבַזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ פָּרָשַׁת קֹרַח קע״ח רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב׳: "הוּא" — דָּא עַתִּיקָא, שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מִקּוֹמַת אָדָם וְהַשָּׂגָתוֹ בַּחָכְמָה שֶׁבְּמֹחוֹ, דְּעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ: "בַּמֻּפְלָא מִמְּךָ וְגוֹמֵר" כַּיָּדוּעַ], וְאֵינוֹ דָּבָר אַחֵר, רַק הַכֹּל אֶחָד [וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּתִּקּוּנִים (סוֹף תִּקּוּן ס״ט) דְּמַאן דְּנָטֵיל מַלְכוּת בְּלֹא תֵּשַׁע סְפִירוֹת, אוֹ תֵּשַׁע סְפִירוֹת בְּלֹא מַלְכוּת, הוּא מְקַצֵּץ בַּנְּטִיעוֹת אוֹ כּוֹפֵר בָּעִקָּר; וְהַמְכֻוָּן לְעִנְיַן דִּיצִיאַת מִצְרַיִם שֶׁהָיָה בְּמוֹרָא גָּדוֹל, זוֹ גִּלּוּי שְׁכִינָה, הָיָה הַהַמְשָׁכָה מֵרֵישׁ כָּל דַּרְגִּין, שֹׁרֶשׁ הַנֶּעְלָם שֶׁשָּׁם דְּבוּקִים הַנְּפָשׁוֹת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל בְּשָׁרְשָׁן, בְּסוֹד תְּפִלִּין שֶׁבְּרֹאשׁ דְּמָארֵי עָלְמָא דִּכְתִיב בְּהוּ: "וּמִי כְּעַמְּךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל וְגוֹמֵר", כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (ו׳ עַמּוּד א׳), וְסוֹד קֶשֶׁר שֶׁל תְּפִלִּין שֶׁהֶרְאָהוּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם כְּשֶׁאָמַר לוֹ: "וְרָאִיתָ אֶת אֲחֹרָי", וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ לְהַאֲרִיךְ].
records.targetEnglish: Once, on the first festival day of Pesach, I dreamt an explanation of the Haggadah’s words, “I am He, and no other.” The level of “I,” the lowest level, the mystery of the Divine Presence [which dwells within the hearts of Israel until one can say “I” in Hashem’s name], as is known, is itself the level of “He,” the highest, hidden level, the mystery of the supernal Keter [in the holy Zohar, Korach 178b, “He” is Atika, which is above the human stature and the grasp of the wisdom in the brain; concerning this they said, “What is too wondrous for you,” and so forth, as is known]. It is not something else; all is one [as stated in the Tikkunim, at the end of Tikkun 69, that one who takes Malkhut without the nine sefirot, or the nine sefirot without Malkhut, cuts the plantings or denies the root. As applied to the Exodus, which occurred “with great awe”—this is the revelation of the Divine Presence—the flow came from the head of all levels, the hidden root where the souls of Israel are attached at their source. This is the mystery of the head tefillin of the Master of the world, in which is written, “Who is like Your people Israel,” and so forth, as stated in Berakhot 6a; and the mystery of the knot of the tefillin which the Holy One, blessed be He, showed Moses when He said to him, “You shall see My back.” This is not the place to elaborate].
records.explanation: Divrei Chalomot gives a positive formulation of the unity that the two errors in Sichat Shedim break apart. The revealed “I” of the Divine Presence and the hidden “He” of the highest root are one; the Exodus makes that unity manifest through the flow from the hidden root into revelation. The connection therefore explains both sides of the distinction, rather than merely repeating the technical names of the errors.
records.translationProvenance: New English translations prepared for this conceptual connection, checked phrase by phrase against the quoted canonical Hebrew. Both complete sections of Sichat Shedim and each complete target paragraph were read; relevance, context, and quotation boundaries were reviewed separately from integrity tests.

records.themeTitle: Lasting unity requires a common divine root
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok contrasts Abraham’s beginning of a holy people and a permanent earthly place for holiness with the generation of the Tower. Their shared language and fixed tower imitate the external form of the unity beginning through Abraham.
records.originHebrew: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר, כִּי הֵם הָיוּ הַקְּלִפָּה הַמְסַבֶּבֶת לַפְּרִי לְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהוּא הָיָה הַפְּרִי הַטּוֹב בַּדּוֹר הַהוּא, וְהֵם הָיוּ בָּרָע זֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה. וְהוּא הַתְחָלַת בִּנְיַן הַקְּדֻשָּׁה, וּמִמֶּנּוּ נִבְנָה גּוֹי אֶחָד בָּאָרֶץ. וְכֵן בִּקְשׁוּ הֵם לְהִתְדַּמּוֹת כְּקוֹף בִּפְנֵי אָדָם, גַּם כֵּן: "שָׂפָה אֶחָת וּדְבָרִים אֲחָדִים" [בְּרֵאשִׁית י״א:א׳]. וְגַם הַתְחָלַת הֶאָרַת הַשָּׂגַת מְקוֹם בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ, הֱיוֹת מִשְׁכָּן קָבוּעַ לַקְּדֻשָּׁה בָּאָרֶץ, הָיָה בְּאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (פְּסָחִים פ״ח עַמּוּד א׳) שֶׁקְּרָאוֹ "הַר", שֶׁהוּא הָרִאשׁוֹן שֶׁהִרְגִּישׁ בְּדָבָר זֶה. וְכֵן הֵם לְעֻמַּת זֶה רָצוּ לִבְנוֹת מִגְדָּל, מָקוֹם קָבוּעַ לָהֶם, וְזֶה הָיָה בְּבָבֶל שֶׁהוּא מַמָּשׁ אֲחוֹרַיִם דְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל וּלְעֻמָּתָהּ,
records.originEnglish: As I have written elsewhere, they were the husk surrounding the fruit that was our father Abraham, peace be upon him. He was the good fruit of that generation, while they were its evil counterpart. He was the beginning of the building of holiness, and from him was built one nation in the land. They too sought to imitate, like an ape before a human: “one language and the same words” (Genesis 11:1). The first illumination of an understanding of the place of the Temple, as a fixed dwelling for holiness on earth, also came through our father Abraham. As our Sages said (Pesachim 88a), he called it a mountain: he was the first to perceive this. Opposite this, they too wished to build a tower, a fixed place for themselves. This was in Babylon, which is precisely the reverse side and counterpart of the Land of Israel.
records.targetHebrew: וְהַתְחָלַת הִתְעוֹרְרוּת אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הָיָה בְּדוֹר הַפְלָגָה שֶׁהֵם הָיוּ הַחֲשׁוֹכָא שֶׁקּוֹדֵם לִנְהוֹרָא שֶׁהִתְעוֹרְרוּ גַּם כֵּן בְּמִדַּת הָאַהֲבָה דְּרֵעִים וְאוֹהֲבִים זֶה לָזֶה לִהְיוֹת עַם אֶחָד, וְחָשְׁבוּ לִהְיוֹת ״גּוֹי אֶחָד בָּאָרֶץ״ (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א י״ז:כ״א) אֶלָּא שֶׁהֵם חָשְׁבוּ לְהַפְרִיד עַצְמָם מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְלִמְרוֹד בְּמַלְכוּת שָׁמָיִם וְדָבָר זֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר: לִהְיוֹת אֶחָד לְמַטָּה וְנִפְרָדִים מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כִּי אֵין יִחוּד אֶלָּא כְּשֶׁמְּיוּחָדִים בִּמְקוֹרָם בַּה׳ אֶחָד, וְהוּא הַמְאַחֵד כָּל הַנִּבְרָאִים אֲבָל בְּעָלְמָא דְּפֵירוּדָא שֶׁנִּפְרָדִים מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, הֵם נִפְרָדִים זֶה מִזֶּה גַּם כֵּן וְרַק אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהִכִּיר יִחוּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְנִקְרָא ״אֹהֲבִי״ (יְשַׁעְיָה מ״א:ח׳) עַל יְדֵי אַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ זוֹכֶה גַּם כֵּן לְאַהֲבַת הַבְּרִיּוֹת, שֶׁכָּל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ לֹא נִבְרָא אֶלָּא לְצַוּוֹת לוֹ (בְּרָכוֹת ו׳ עַמּוּד ב׳) שֶׁכְּמוֹ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יְחִידִי בָּעֶלְיוֹנִים, כָּךְ הוּא יָחִיד בַּתַּחְתּוֹנִים כְּאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן קוֹדֶם הַחֵטְא וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כ״א:ה׳) עַל פָּסוּק ״[הֵן] הָאָדָם הָיָה כְּאַחַד מִמֶּנּוּ״ (בְּרֵאשִׁית ג:כב) וְכָל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ הֵם אֵבְרֵי קוֹמָתוֹ, וְזָכָה לְהוֹלִיד ״גּוֹי אֶחָד״ אֲבָל הֵם שֶׁרָצוּ לְהִתְדַּמּוֹת בְּאַהֲבָתָם כְּקוֹף בִּפְנֵי אָדָם וְלִהְיוֹת גַּם כֵּן ״עַם אֶחָד״, לֹא עָלְתָה בְּיָדָם כִּי אַדְּרַבָּא זֶה עַצְמוֹ שֶׁחָשְׁבוּ לְהִתְיַיחֵד עַל יְדֵי זֶה, עַל יְדֵי הָעִיר וְהַמִּגְדָּל — גָּרַם פֵּירוּדָם דְּנִתְבָּרַר דְּ״נַהֲפוֹךְ הוּא״ (אֶסְתֵּר ט:א), דְּ״בְּחֻמָּם אָשִׁית אֶת מִשְׁתֵּיהֶם״ (יִרְמְיָה נ״א:ל״ט) כִּי כָל חִבּוּרָם הוּא לְזִמָּה וּלְתַאֲווֹת רָעוֹת וְסוֹף שֶׁבָּטֵל דָּבָר — וּבָטְלָה אַהֲבָה (אָבוֹת ה:טז):
records.targetEnglish: The beginning of our father Abraham’s awakening was in the generation of the Dispersion, who were the darkness preceding the light. They too awakened to the quality of love, as companions who loved one another, to become one people, intending to be “one nation in the land” (I Chronicles 17:21). But they intended to separate themselves from Hashem and rebel against the kingdom of Heaven. This is impossible: to be one below while separated from Hashem. There is unity only when they are united at their source in the one Hashem, who unites all creatures. But in the world of separation, when they are separated from Hashem, they are also separated from one another. Only our father Abraham, who recognized Hashem’s unity and was called “the one who loves Me” (Isaiah 41:8), merits love of creatures through love of Hashem: the entire world was created only to provide him companionship (Berakhot 6b). Just as Hashem is unique among the higher beings, so he is unique among the lower beings, like Adam before the sin, as they said about “Behold, the human has become like one of us” (Genesis 3:22). The whole world consists of the limbs of his stature, and he merited to give rise to one nation. But those who wished to imitate through their love, like an ape before a human, and also become one people, did not succeed. On the contrary, the very thing through which they intended to unite—the city and the tower—caused their separation. It became clear that the opposite was true: “In their heat I will set their feasts” (Jeremiah 51:39), because all their joining was for depravity and corrupt desires. In the end, when the thing ceased, the love ceased (Avot 5:16).
records.explanation: Machshavot Charutz identifies the decisive difference between the two outwardly similar projects. Common language, affection, and a shared building cannot sustain unity while their participants detach themselves from the divine source that unites their lives. Abraham’s love of creatures follows from recognition of that source. This explains why Sichat Shedim calls the Tower an imitation of Abraham’s work and why the imitation produces division.

records.themeTitle: Patient building after the first awakening
records.themeSummary: Sichat Shedim contrasts the patience of divine building with the Tower generation’s rush to make its imitation actual. The premature imitation collapses, while the light awakening through Abraham develops toward an enduring future.
records.originHebrew: וְאָז זֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה נִתְעוֹרְרוּ הֵם גַּם כֵּן לְיַסֵּד הַמִּגְדָּל, רַק שֶׁאֵצֶל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא בִּמְתִינוּת, וְאֶצְלָם בִּמְהִירוּת, "וְעַד אַרְגִּיעָה לְשׁוֹן שָׁקֶר" [מִשְׁלֵי י״ב:י״ט], "כָּלָה עָנָן וַיֵּלַךְ" [אִיּוֹב ז׳:ט׳], "כְּצֵל יָעוּף". לְפִיכָךְ הִתְחִילוּ מִיָּד לְהוֹצִיא לַפֹּעַל, וְעַל יְדֵי הַהוֹצָאָה לַפֹּעַל נִתְבַּטֵּל, כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל דְּקִדֵּשׁ הַיּוֹם. וְאָמַר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ: "הָבָה נֵרְדָה וְגוֹמֵר" [בְּרֵאשִׁית י״א:ז׳], וְזָרַח בְּיוֹתֵר אוֹרוֹ שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם. כִּי לְעוֹלָם כְּשֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מַתְחִיל לְחַדֵּשׁ דָּבָר, אָז הוּא מִתְפַּשֵּׁט בְּכָל הָעוֹלָמוֹת וְעַד שֶׁמַּגִּיעַ גַּם לְעֵץ הַדַּעַת טוֹב וָרָע וּלְעוֹלָם הַזֶּה. וְגַם כֹּחוֹת הָרָע שֶׁיִּסֵּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לִהְיוֹת לָהֶם מְצִיאוּת דִּמְיוֹנִי קוֹלְטִים גַּם כֵּן אוֹתוֹ דְּבַר הִתְחַדְּשׁוּת וְעוֹשִׂים גַּם כֵּן כֵּן; רַק לִהְיוֹתוֹ זֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה הוּא מַמָּשׁ לְהֵיפֶךְ, וְלִהְיוֹתוֹ מִפְּעֻלַּת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לִהְיוֹת כֵּן: בְּרֵישָׁא חֲשׁוֹכָא וַהֲדַר נְהוֹרָא [שַׁבָּת ע״ז עַמּוּד ב׳], כִּי יִתְרוֹן הָאוֹר נִכָּר רַק מִן הַחֹשֶׁךְ, לָכֵן הֵם מַתְחִילִים לִפְעֹל קֹדֶם. וּמִזֶּה זוֹרֵחַ הָאוֹר, כְּטַעַם: "יָשֶׁת חֹשֶׁךְ סִתְרוֹ" [תְּהִלִּים י״ח:י״ב], כִּי שָׁם הוּא נִסְתָּר. וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי, כִּי הַתְחָלַת הַכָּרַת אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אֶת בּוֹרְאוֹ הָיָה מִצַּד הַפֶּלֶא דְּחִלּוּק הַלְּשׁוֹנוֹת שֶׁרָאָה, וְתֵכֶף: "יִתְפָּרְדוּ כָּל פֹּעֲלֵי אָוֶן" [תְּהִלִּים צ״ב:י׳], "וַתְּרוֹמַמְנָה קַרְנוֹת צַדִּיק" [שָׁם ע״ה:י״א], עַל דֶּרֶךְ: "וּשְׂפַת אֱמֶת תִּכּוֹן לָעַד" [מִשְׁלֵי י״ב:י״ט], כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ: "כּוֹנַנְתָּ" לֹא כְתִיב, רַק לְשׁוֹן עָתִיד. כִּי פְּעֻלַּת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בִּמְתִינוּת; מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הֵם לְהֵיפֶךְ, הֵם בַּהֹוֶה, רַק שֶׁאֵין לוֹ קִיּוּם רַק עַד אַרְגִּיעָה.
records.originEnglish: Then, as a counterpart, they too were stirred to lay the foundation of the Tower. But with Hashem it proceeds patiently, while with them it proceeds in haste: “A lying tongue is but for a moment” (Proverbs 12:19), “A cloud vanishes and goes” (Job 7:9), “It flies away like a shadow.” They therefore began at once to bring it into action; through being brought into action it was annulled, as explained above when the day became holy. Hashem said, “Come, let us descend,” and so forth (Genesis 11:7), and the light of our father Abraham shone more greatly. Whenever the Holy One, blessed be He, begins to bring something new, it spreads through all the worlds until it reaches the Tree of Knowledge of good and evil and this world. The powers of evil, which Hashem established to have an imagined existence, also absorb that new thing and act in the same way. But as a counterpart it is the exact opposite. Hashem’s action arranged that darkness comes first and light afterward, for the advantage of light is recognizable only from darkness; therefore they begin to act first. From this the light shines, in the sense of “He made darkness His hiding place” (Psalms 18:12), for there it is concealed. As I have written, Abraham’s beginning of recognizing his Creator came through the wonder of the division of languages that he saw. Immediately, “All workers of iniquity shall be scattered” (Psalms 92:10), and “The horns of the righteous shall be raised” (Psalms 75:11), in the manner of “The lip of truth shall be established forever” (Proverbs 12:19). As the holy Zohar says, it is not written “has been established,” but in the future tense. Hashem’s action proceeds patiently. With them it is the opposite: they act in the present, but it endures only for a moment.
records.targetHebrew: רֵאשִׁית כְּנִיסַת הָאָדָם לַעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת בְּחִפָּזוֹן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ בְּפֶסַח מִצְרַיִם שֶׁהָיָה נֶאֱכָל בְּחִפָּזוֹן, וְלֹא פֶּסַח דּוֹרוֹת. מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהַהַתְחָלָה לְנַתֵּק עַצְמוֹ מִכָּל תַּאֲווֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁהוּא מְקֻשָּׁר בָּהֶם, צָרִיךְ לִשְׁמֹר הָרֶגַע שֶׁמִּתְעוֹרֵר בּוֹ רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם, וְלַחְפּוֹז עַל אוֹתוֹ רֶגַע לְמַהֵר לָצֵאת מֵהֶם, אוּלַי יוּכַל. וְאַחַר כָּךְ שׁוּב יֵלֵךְ בִּמְתִינוּת וּלְאַט, כְּדִין פֶּסַח דּוֹרוֹת.
records.targetEnglish: A person’s first entry into the service of Hashem must be in haste, as we find concerning the Pesach offering in Egypt, which was eaten in haste, unlike the Pesach offering of later generations. At the beginning, to detach himself from all the desires of this world to which he is bound, he must guard the moment when a desire for Hashem awakens within him, and hasten upon that moment to hurry out of them, if he can. Afterward he should again proceed patiently and slowly, as is the law of the Pesach offering of later generations.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik distinguishes the brief urgency needed to leave an existing attachment from the patient progress that follows. That distinction clarifies the criticism of haste in Sichat Shedim: the Tower generation rushes to complete its own construction, while enduring holy building unfolds patiently. The comparison preserves the legitimate initial haste of awakening and keeps it distinct from premature completion.

records.themeTitle: The three soul powers and their bodily expression
records.themeSummary: To explain what distinguishes the human soul from bodily animal life, Rav Tzadok invokes nefesh, ruach, and neshamah and explicitly refers to Sichat Malakhei HaSharet. The body and these soul powers play different roles in his account of the Tower generation’s transformation.
records.originHebrew: וּבְכָל אָדָם יֵשׁ גּוּף הַחַי עַל יְדֵי כֹּחַ גּוּפָנִי וְנֶפֶשׁ הַבְּהֵמִית, שֶׁבָּזֶה דּוֹמֶה לִבְהֵמָה; וְגַם נֶפֶשׁ הַכְּלוּלָה מִנֶּפֶשׁ, רוּחַ, נְשָׁמָה, שֶׁהִיא כֹּחַ הַנֶּפֶשׁ שֶׁבָּאָדָם הַנְּתוּנָה בְּמֹחַ, וְלֵב, וְכָבֵד, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּקֻנְטְרֵס "שִׂיחַת מַלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת", שֶׁהֵם נֶגֶד אַרְבָּעָה פַרְצוּפִין. וְהַגּוּף נִשְׁתַּנָּה לְקוֹף, כִּנְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר לְאַרְיֵה, שֶׁכָּךְ מִטֶּבַע הָאָדָם כְּשֶׁיִּהְיֶה זֶה בֵּין הַבַּעֲלֵי חַיִּים וְיִסְתַּלֵּק דַּעְתּוֹ מִמֶּנּוּ. וְחֶלְקֵי נֶפֶשׁ, רוּחַ, נְשָׁמָה שֶׁלָּהֶם, שֶׁהוּא הִשְׁתַּנּוּת שֶׁל אָדָם מִן הַקּוֹף, זֶה נִיטַל מֵהֶם וְנַעֲשָׂה מִזֶּה רוּחִין, וְשֵׁדִין, וְלִילִין. וְהַיְינוּ כִּי רוּחִין, וְשֵׁדִין, וְלִילִין הֵם מַמָּשׁ דֻּגְמַת נֶפֶשׁ, רוּחַ, נְשָׁמָה שֶׁל הָאָדָם, וּלְכָךְ הֵם נַעֲשִׂים מֵהַטִּפֵּי זֶרַע כְּמַאֲמָרָם זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּעֵירוּבִין [י״ח עַמּוּד ב׳]; שֶׁהֲרֵי גַּם בָּהֶם יֵשׁ כֹּחַ נֶפֶשׁ, רוּחַ, נְשָׁמָה שֶׁל הָאָדָם, שֶׁאִלּוּ בָּאוּ בְּנוּקְבָא הָיוּ נוֹלָד מִזֶּה אָדָם חַי בְּנֶפֶשׁ, רוּחַ, נְשָׁמָה.
records.originEnglish: Every person has a body that lives through bodily power and an animal soul, in which he resembles an animal. He also has a soul comprising nefesh, ruach, and neshamah: the power of the human soul situated in the brain, heart, and liver, as I wrote in the booklet Sichat Malakhei HaSharet; these correspond to four configurations. The body changed into an ape, as Nebuchadnezzar changed into a lion, for this is part of human nature when a person is among the animals and his understanding departs from him. Their portions of nefesh, ruach, and neshamah, which distinguish the human from the ape, were taken from them, and from them were made ruchin, shedin, and lilin. These are precisely counterparts of the human nefesh, ruach, and neshamah; therefore they are made from drops of seed, as our Sages said in Eruvin 18b. Those drops too contain the power of the human nefesh, ruach, and neshamah, for had they entered the female, a living human with nefesh, ruach, and neshamah would have been born.
records.targetHebrew: כִּי שְׁלֹשָׁה כֹחוֹת בָּאָדָם: מַחֲשָׁבָה, דִּבּוּר וּמַעֲשֶׂה; הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה בַּמֹּחַ וְהוּא הַחָכְמָה שֶׁבּוֹ, וְהַדִּבּוּר בַּלֵּב שֶׁהוּא הַכּוֹלֵל כָּל אֵבָרִים הַפְּנִימִיִּים שֶׁמֵּהֶם הַדִּבּוּר יוֹצֵא, וְכֵן אֵצֶל הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב שַׁיָּךְ דִּבּוּר שֶׁהוּא גָּלוּי קְצָת, שֶׁכְּבָר הוּא מְגֻלֶּה יוֹתֵר אֵצֶל אֵבְרֵי גוּפוֹ, וְהַיְינוּ עַל יְדֵי הַהַרְגָּשָׁה שֶׁבַּלֵּב הוּא כֹּחַ הַהַרְגָּשָׁה וְכָל אֵבָרִים מַרְגִּישִׁים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכְּשֶׁיַּחְשֹׁב בְּלִבּוֹ עִנְיַן צַעַר כָּל הָאֵבָרִים מִצְטַעֲרִים; מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה וְהַחָכְמָה שֶׁבַּמֹּחַ הוּא בְּהֶעְלֵם שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְגֻלֶּה אַף לְאֵבְרֵי הַגּוּף, רַק לַמֹּחַ בִּלְבַד. וְהַמַּעֲשֶׂה הוּא בָּאֵבָרִים הַחִיצוֹנִים כְּלֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה שֶׁבַּגּוּף, שֶׁמְּקוֹרָם הַכָּבֵד שֶׁהוּא מְקוֹר הַדָּם כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא (חֻלִּין ק״ט עַמּוּד ב׳), וְהַדָּם הוּא עִקַּר חִיּוּת אֵבְרֵי הַגּוּף כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (דְּבָרִים י״ב:כ״ג): "כִּי הַדָּם הוּא הַנָּפֶשׁ". וְהֵם גַּם כֵּן ג׳ כֹּחוֹת הַנֶּפֶשׁ שֶׁבָּאָדָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַאֲבַ״ע סוֹף פָּרָשַׁת מִשְׁפָּטִים [שְׁמוֹת כ״ג:כ״ה], שֶׁמִּשְׁכַּן הַנְּשָׁמָה בַּמֹּחַ, וְהָרוּחַ בַּלֵּב, וְהַנֶּפֶשׁ בַּכָּבֵד, יְעֻיַּן שָׁם; וְכָל דְּבָרִים אֵלּוּ מְבֹאָרִים אֶצְלֵנוּ בִּמְקוֹמָן בַּאֲרִיכוּת.
records.targetEnglish: There are three powers in the human: thought, speech, and action. Thought is in the brain and is the wisdom within it. Speech is in the heart, which includes all the internal organs from which speech emerges. Speech also applies to thought in the heart, for it is somewhat revealed: it is already more apparent to the organs of the body. This occurs through feeling in the heart, the power of sensation, and all the organs feel it; when a person thinks of something distressing in his heart, all the organs are distressed. By contrast, the thought and wisdom in the brain remain concealed, revealed only to the brain and not even to the organs of the body. Action is in the external organs, the body’s instruments of action, whose source is the liver, the source of blood, as stated in Chullin 109b. Blood is the essential life of the body’s organs, as it is said, “For the blood is the nefesh” (Deuteronomy 12:23). These are also the three powers of the human soul, as Ibn Ezra wrote at the end of Mishpatim (Exodus 23:25): the neshamah dwells in the brain, the ruach in the heart, and the nefesh in the liver; see there. All these matters are explained at length in their appropriate places in our writings.
records.explanation: This is a substantive passage from the work Sichat Shedim explicitly cites. It explains the brain, heart, and liver through thought, speech, and action and through increasing degrees of manifestation. The mapping makes the difference between bodily animal life and the three human soul powers intelligible in the author’s own terms. The selected passage explains the three powers; it does not independently resolve the adjoining reference to four configurations.

records.themeTitle: The covenant reveals an inner holiness
records.themeSummary: Sichat Shedim connects the bodily sign of the covenant with the distinction made visible through human action. Removing the covering reveals what the author describes as the true and holy inner foundation.
records.originHebrew: וְהַחִלּוּק הוּא רַק בְּשֵׁדִין, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא בִּנְדָרִים (ל״א עַמּוּד ב׳): שֶׁאֵין הָעָרְלָה נִקְרֵאת אֶלָּא עַל שֵׁם אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם; שֶׁכָּל הַחִלּוּק בֵּין יִשְׂרָאֵל לְאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם הוּא רַק בְּאוֹת בְּרִית, שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַחִלּוּק בְּגוּפָם בֵּין גּוּף זֶה לָזֶה, וְנַעֲשָׂה עַל יְדֵי פְּעֻלַּת הָאָדָם שֶׁהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת הוּא הַגּוֹרֵם, וְעַל יְדֵי פְּעֻלָּתוֹ וְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ נַעֲשָׂה הִשְׁתַּנּוּת בַּגּוּף בַּיְסוֹד. רָצָה לוֹמַר, שֶׁזֶּה הַיְסוֹד שֶׁקֶר, וְזֶה הַיְסוֹד שֶׁלּוֹ הוּא אֱמֶת וְקָדוֹשׁ, וְזֶה עַל יְדֵי שֶׁנִּתְגַּלָּה הַלְּבוּשׁ שֶׁעָלָיו מֵעָרְלָה וּקְלִפָּה הַחוֹפֶפֶת, שֶׁזֶּהוּ עִקַּר הָאֱמֶת כַּאֲשֶׁר מִתְגַּלֶּה הַפְּרִי מִן הַקְּלִפָּה הַמְכַסֵּית וּמַאֲפִילָה.
records.originEnglish: The distinction is only in the shedin, as stated in Nedarim 31b: the term “uncircumcision” is applied only in reference to the nations of the world. The entire distinction between Israel and the nations is in the sign of the covenant; this distinguishes one body from another. It is made through human action, for effort is what brings it about: through a person’s action and effort, a change is made in the body, in Yesod. This means that one foundation is false, while the other’s foundation is true and holy. This comes through the removal of the garment of foreskin and husk covering it. This is the essential truth, when the fruit is revealed from the husk that covers and darkens it.
records.targetHebrew: אֲבָל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, דַּאֲפִילּוּ עֲרֵלִים נִקְרְאוּ מוּלִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּנְדָרִים (ל״א עַמּוּד ב׳), אֵין בָּהֶם עוֹד פְּסֹלֶת מְחֻבָּר לְעֶצֶם גּוּפָם כְּלָל; רַק הַפְּסֹלֶת לָהֶם כְּבֶטֶן הַמְּלֵאָה וּמַעֲלָה סִרְחוֹן, וּכְשֶׁנִּפְנָה וְיָצָא הַפְּסֹלֶת הַמַּסְרִיחַ מִקֶּרֶב גּוּפָן — עָבַר הַמּוּם; וְאֵין שׁוּם פְּסֹלֶת וְסִרְחוֹן בִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵעַצְמִיּוּתָם, רַק דָּבָר אֶחָד יֵשׁ בְּקֶרֶב גּוּפָם הַמַּסְרִיחַ, וּבְקִרְבָּם כֹּחַ הַדּוֹחֶה לִדְחוֹתוֹ וּלְהוֹצִיאוֹ בְּעַל כָּרְחוֹ מִגּוּפוֹ וְיָסוּר הַסִּרְחוֹן
records.targetEnglish: But the children of Israel, even when uncircumcised, are called circumcised, as they said in Nedarim 31b. No refuse remains attached to the essence of their body at all. Rather, their refuse is like a belly that is full and gives off a foul smell; when it is emptied and the foul refuse leaves the body, the blemish passes away. No refuse or foulness in the children of Israel comes from their essence. There is only something within their body that gives off a foul smell, and within them is a power to reject it and expel it from the body against its will, so that the foulness departs.
records.explanation: Divrei Chalomot distinguishes a person’s essential covenantal identity from an impurity that can enter and must be expelled. This explains the force of revealing the fruit beneath its covering in Sichat Shedim: the act discloses an inner holiness instead of creating holiness from nothing. The full target paragraph also stresses that an internal impurity can be especially offensive and drive away the Divine Presence, so the distinction does not make the blemish insignificant.
records.translationProvenance: New English translations prepared for this conceptual connection, checked phrase by phrase against the quoted canonical Hebrew. Both complete sections of Sichat Shedim and each complete target paragraph were read; relevance, context, and quotation boundaries were reviewed separately from integrity tests.
